extracted.intended_audience: aspiring middle-grade/young-adult writers, educators, and readers interested in myth-based fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing middle-grade/YA novels that weave mythology into contemporary stories—covering research, voice, representation, and series continuity. Geared toward authors producing myth-inspired children's fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and fact-checking of mythologies
rubrics_metrics.description: “I always review the myths I’ll be writing about and check my facts as I work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do a month (or appropriate period) of research before/during drafting; review primary myths and verify facts continually rather than relying on memory. Treat research as integral to shaping the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and account for source limitations (especially Norse)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Norse is far more challenging, simply because our primary sources are so limited. The Vikings were not big writers. We have to rely on fewer sources, most of which were written centuries after the Viking Age.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about gaps in the source material and factor limited or late sources into decisions about fidelity and reconstruction. Different mythic traditions will require different research strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patch gaps with educated guesswork while preserving original worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: When sources have holes, use “educated guesswork using more recent Scandinavian folklore or other Germanic traditions, trying to recapture the ‘DNA’ of the original Old Norse worldview.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use related folklore, comparative traditions, and informed invention to fill gaps, but aim to preserve the core sensibilities and worldview of the original mythology rather than inventing superficially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain distinct narrator/character voices
rubrics_metrics.description: “I find that the narrators’ voices are really very different… As for Apollo/Lester, he’s in a class by himself. His voice is VERY different from either Magnus or Percy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each narrator/protagonist has a unique voice so readers can distinguish them easily—especially important when characters from different series or books meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write authentic voice for the target age ('native teenage prose')
rubrics_metrics.description: Riordan’s signature ability: “write almost native teenage prose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for authenticity in diction, tone, and perspective appropriate to the age of the protagonist; read and immerse yourself in contemporary teen speech and attitudes to capture that voice convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reading as a palate cleanser and research method between projects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reading is an excellent palate cleanser. I usually go into research mode for about a month, reading for the new project and also reading unrelated books. I’m a big fan of history, science fiction, and fantasy, though my taste is pretty eclectic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate targeted research reading with unrelated reading to refresh perspective; diversify reading (history, sci-fi, fantasy) to feed ideas and avoid creative fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and inclusion of diverse identities
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have made a conscious effort to expand on the representation in my books, because I want all kinds of kids to find themselves in these stories and know that they too can be heroes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally include diverse characters and identities so readers from varied backgrounds can see themselves; representation should be meaningful (characters not erased) and treated with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cultural appropriation; amplify authentic cultural voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Riordan did not want “to poach or appropriate cultures that weren’t mine and that I didn’t fully understand,” so he started an imprint to find writers from diverse, under-represented backgrounds to tell their own myth-based stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are not from a culture, be cautious about claiming its stories; consider supporting or foregrounding authors from that culture rather than attempting to represent it yourself. Use platform to elevate authentic voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan series continuity and character crossovers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trials of Apollo series is “meant to be a chance for fans to revisit all their friends from the first two Greek/Roman series… so all the characters… will eventually make appearances.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing multiple interrelated series, plan character appearances and continuity so crossovers feel natural and voices remain consistent; anticipate future meetings and plan pacing and characterization accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot like a puzzle: know the general picture then sort pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s like working on a puzzle. You know what the general picture is going to look like when it’s all assembled. It’s just a matter of sorting out the pieces and figuring out which ones to use where.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline or hold a clear overall arc in mind, then assemble scenes and elements to fit that picture; choose which pieces to use and where to reveal them to create a coherent narrative.
